tips.title: Each one needs its own list of details
tips.body: A **translation** needs a vector. A **reflection** needs the equation of the mirror line. A **rotation** needs a centre, an angle **and** a direction. An **enlargement** needs a centre and a scale factor. Leaving one out is the most common way to lose a mark in this topic.

tips.title: The centre of enlargement is the point that does not move
tips.body: To find it, join each vertex of the image to the matching vertex of the object and extend the lines. They all cross at one point, and that is the centre. It works for fractional and negative scale factors too, which is when guessing stops working.

tips.title: Three of the four keep the shape identical
tips.body: Translations, reflections and rotations are **congruent** transformations: the image is the same size and shape, just somewhere else. Only an **enlargement** changes the size. So if the image is a different size, no amount of sliding, flipping or turning will describe it.

tips.title: Area scales by the square of the scale factor
tips.body: An enlargement of scale factor $k$ multiplies every **length** by $k$ and every **area** by $k^2$. Scale factor $2$ makes the area $4$ times bigger; scale factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$ makes it $4$ times smaller. Use it to check an enlargement you have drawn.

why.matters:
Four moves cover everything the topic asks for, and three of them — translation, reflection, rotation — leave the shape **congruent**: same size, same angles, somewhere else. Only an **enlargement** changes the size, and then every length is multiplied by $k$ and every area by $k^2$.

What makes that worth more than a sketching trick is the second half: knowing which properties survive. A translated, reflected or rotated shape has the same lengths and angles as the one you started with, so anything you proved about one is true of the other without doing it again.

examples.title: The word on the front of an ambulance
examples.body:
AMBULANCE is painted reversed across the bonnet so that it reads the right way round in a driver's mirror. The mirror is doing a **reflection**, and the paint undoes it in advance.

What is easy to miss is that only some of the letters need reversing at all. A, M, U and the second A are symmetric about a vertical line, so a mirror leaves them exactly as they are. B, L, N, C and E are not, so those five are the ones that come back wrong — 4 letters of the 9 survive untouched.

That is the whole idea of an invariant point, one word wide: a reflection moves the shape, and anything lying on the mirror line — or symmetric about it — stays put.

examples.title: Why you are never upside down on a big wheel
examples.body:
The wheel turns through a full circle, so it would be reasonable to expect the cabin at the top to be upside down. It never is, and the reason is that the cabin is not being rotated at all.

Each cabin hangs from a bearing and is held level, so as the wheel goes round the cabin is **translated** — moved without turning. Every point of it shifts by the same vector, and the floor stays the floor. The wheel is rotating; its passengers are not.

That is the difference between the two transformations, built into a machine. A rotation turns every point about a centre, so orientation changes; a translation moves every point the same way, so orientation cannot. A fairground ride that *does* rotate its cars is a different ride, and you can feel which is which.

examples.title: Why the photocopier offers 141%
examples.body:
The enlarge button on a copier offers 141% for A4 to A3 and 71% for A4 to A5, and neither number is arbitrary. A4 is 210 by 297 mm and A3 is 297 by 420, so the scale factor is $420/297 \approx \sqrt{2}$ — about 1.414, or 141% to the nearest whole number.

The point of choosing that factor is what it does to the **area**. An enlargement multiplies area by $k^2$, and $(\sqrt{2})^2 = 2$ exactly, so A3 holds precisely twice the paper of A4: 623.7 cm² against 1247.4. Every A size works this way, which is why cutting a sheet in half gives the next size down rather than an awkward shape.

It is also why a copy scaled by eye goes wrong. Setting 200% to "double the page" gives four times the area, and three quarters of it lands off the paper.

steps.title: Four transformations, and what each one needs
steps.body:
A **transformation** moves a shape to a new position. There are four at GCSE, and the first job is always to name the right one.

- A **translation** slides the shape. Nothing turns and nothing flips.
- A **reflection** flips it in a mirror line.
- A **rotation** turns it about a point.
- An **enlargement** changes its size.

> Three of the four leave the shape **congruent** — identical in size and shape. Only an **enlargement** changes the size.

That is the fastest first check. If the image is a different size from the object, the answer must be an enlargement, and no amount of sliding or turning will do.

**Each transformation needs its own details**, and a description is not complete without them.

- Translation: the **vector**, written as a column, $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ — across first, then up.
- Reflection: the **equation of the mirror line**, such as $x = 2$ or $y = x$.
- Rotation: the **centre**, the **angle**, and the **direction**.
- Enlargement: the **centre** and the **scale factor**.

Throughout this topic the object is triangle $A$ with vertices $(1, 1)$, $(4, 1)$ and $(1, 3)$.

check.solution: Add $3$ to the $x$ coordinate and $2$ to the $y$: $(4 + 3, 1 + 2) = (7, 3)$.

steps.title: Rotations
steps.body:
A **rotation** turns the shape about a fixed point, the **centre of rotation**. Three things are needed to describe one: the centre, the angle, and the direction.

> Always say **clockwise** or **anticlockwise**. The only exception is $180°$, where both give the same answer.

**About the origin**, the three common rotations have a rule each.

| Rotation | $(x, y)$ becomes |
| --- | --- |
| $90°$ clockwise | $(y, -x)$ |
| $90°$ anticlockwise | $(-y, x)$ |
| $180°$ | $(-x, -y)$ |

For triangle $A$ with vertices $(1, 1)$, $(4, 1)$, $(1, 3)$, a rotation of $90°$ **clockwise** about the origin gives $(1, -1)$, $(1, -4)$ and $(3, -1)$. Anticlockwise gives $(-1, 1)$, $(-1, 4)$ and $(-3, 1)$ — a different place entirely, which is why the direction has to be stated.

**Tracing paper is allowed**, and in an exam it is faster and safer than the rules. Trace the shape, put your pencil on the centre, and turn the paper.

**Finding the centre afterwards** is harder. Tracing paper again: put the point of your pencil where you think the centre is and turn — if the traced shape lands on the image, you were right.

A rotation keeps the shape **congruent**. It is the same size, and the same way round: unlike a reflection, nothing is mirrored.

check.solution: With the centre at the origin, multiply both coordinates by the scale factor: $(4 \times 2, 1 \times 2) = (8, 2)$.

steps.title: Fractional and negative scale factors
steps.body:
The word "enlargement" is used even when the shape gets **smaller**. A scale factor between $0$ and $1$ shrinks it.

Scale factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$, centre the origin, takes triangle $A$ to $(0.5, 0.5)$, $(2, 0.5)$ and $(0.5, 1.5)$. Every length is halved, and the area is **quartered**: from $3$ to $0.75$.

> Do not call a shrinking "scale factor $2$". It is scale factor $\tfrac{1}{2}$, and the word enlargement is still correct.

**A negative scale factor** does something more dramatic: the image appears on the **other side of the centre**, and upside down.

Scale factor $-1$, centre the origin, takes $(1, 1)$ to $(-1, -1)$, $(4, 1)$ to $(-4, -1)$ and $(1, 3)$ to $(-1, -3)$.

**Look at those coordinates.** They are exactly what a rotation of $180°$ about the origin would have given. An enlargement of scale factor $-1$ and a half turn about the same point are the **same transformation**, which is a useful thing to notice and a favourite of examiners.

For a negative factor, the rule is the same as ever — multiply the distance from the centre — but the minus sends you backwards through the centre before you measure.

**Area is always positive.** Scale factor $-2$ multiplies area by $(-2)^2 = 4$, not by $-4$.

check.prompt: A shape is enlarged by scale factor $3$. How many times bigger is its area?
check.solution: Lengths are multiplied by $3$, and area involves two lengths, so it is multiplied by $3^2 = 9$. Volume would be multiplied by $3^3 = 27$.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
Triangle $A$ has vertices $(1, 1)$, $(4, 1)$ and $(1, 3)$.

**Part A — carry them out.**

1. Translate $A$ by $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$.
2. Reflect $A$ in the $y$ axis.
3. Reflect $A$ in the line $y = x$.
4. Rotate $A$ by $90°$ clockwise about the origin.

**Part B — enlargements.**

5. Enlarge $A$ by scale factor $2$, centre the origin.
6. Enlarge $A$ by scale factor $2$, centre $(1, 1)$. How is this different from question 5?
7. Enlarge $A$ by scale factor $-1$, centre the origin. What single rotation would have done the same?

**Part C — the one worth thinking hardest about.**

8. Triangle $A$ has area $3$. Write down the area after each of questions 1, 4 and 5, and explain the pattern.

For question 3, reflecting in $y = x$ swaps each pair of coordinates.

check.solution: Reflecting in $y = x$ swaps the coordinates, so $(4, 1)$ becomes $(1, 4)$. The line $y = x$ is the diagonal through the origin, and a point's distance from it is the same on either side.

steps.title: Going deeper: finding a centre, and what two transformations add up to
steps.body:
**Finding the centre of an enlargement.** Do not guess. Join each vertex of the image to the matching vertex of the object, and extend the lines. They all meet at one point, and that is the centre. It works for fractional scale factors and for negative ones, where guessing fails completely.

The scale factor comes from a pair of matching lengths: image length divided by object length. If the image is on the **other side** of the centre, the factor is negative.

**Two transformations can equal one.** This is spec point G8, and it is worth knowing a few.

- Reflect in the $x$ axis, then reflect in the $y$ axis: every point $(x, y)$ becomes $(x, -y)$ and then $(-x, -y)$. That is a **rotation of $180°$ about the origin**.
- An enlargement of scale factor $-1$ about a point is also a **rotation of $180°$** about that point.
- Two translations, one after the other, make a single translation: just add the vectors.
- A rotation of $90°$ clockwise followed by another gives $180°$.

**What stays the same.** Some features survive every transformation and some do not.

| Feature | Translation | Reflection | Rotation | Enlargement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lengths | kept | kept | kept | multiplied by $k$ |
| Angles | kept | kept | kept | kept |
| Area | kept | kept | kept | multiplied by $k^2$ |
| Which way round | kept | **flipped** | kept | kept, unless $k < 0$ |

That last row is the quick test between a rotation and a reflection: a reflection reverses the order of the vertices round the shape, and a rotation does not.

check.prompt: A shape is reflected in the $x$ axis and then reflected in the $y$ axis. What single transformation has the same effect?
check.solution: The first reflection sends $(x, y)$ to $(x, -y)$, and the second sends that to $(-x, -y)$. Both coordinates have changed sign, which is exactly a rotation of $180°$ about the origin. Flipping twice restores the original order of the vertices, which is why the result is a rotation rather than a reflection.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Four transformations: **translation**, **reflection**, **rotation**, **enlargement**.
- Only an **enlargement** changes the size. The other three leave the shape **congruent**.
- **Translation** needs a **vector**: across on top, up underneath.
- **Reflection** needs the **equation** of the mirror line: $x = 2$, $y = -1$, $y = x$.
- **Rotation** needs a **centre**, an **angle** and a **direction**. Only $180°$ needs no direction.
- About the origin: $90°$ clockwise is $(y, -x)$; anticlockwise is $(-y, x)$; $180°$ is $(-x, -y)$.
- **Enlargement** needs a **centre** and a **scale factor**.
- The **centre does not move**. Find it by joining matching vertices and extending.
- A scale factor between $0$ and $1$ makes the shape **smaller**, and it is still an enlargement.
- A **negative** scale factor puts the image on the other side of the centre, upside down.
- Scale factor $-1$ about a point is the same as a **rotation of $180°$** about it.
- Lengths scale by $k$; **areas scale by $k^2$**.
- Reflecting twice in perpendicular lines is a rotation of $180°$.
- A **reflection reverses** which way round the vertices go; a rotation does not.
- Give **one** transformation when one is asked for.

questions.prompt: Which transformation changes the size of a shape?
questions.solution: Only an enlargement changes the size. The other three leave the shape congruent — identical in size and shape — and simply move it.

questions.prompt: What does the vector $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ tell you to do?
questions.solution: In a column vector the **top** number is the movement across and the **bottom** number is the movement up. So $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$ means $3$ right and $2$ up.

questions.prompt: The point $(4, 1)$ is translated by $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$. Give the coordinates of the image.
questions.solution: Add $3$ to the $x$ coordinate and $2$ to the $y$ coordinate: $(7, 3)$.

questions.prompt: The point $(4, 1)$ is reflected in the $y$ axis. What is its image?
questions.solution: The $y$ axis is the line $x = 0$, so reflecting in it changes the sign of the $x$ coordinate and leaves the height alone: $(4, 1)$ becomes $(-4, 1)$.

questions.prompt: A shape is rotated $90°$ about the origin. What else must be given for the description to be complete?
questions.solution: A rotation needs a centre, an angle and a **direction**. Ninety degrees clockwise and ninety degrees anticlockwise land the shape in two different places.

questions.prompt: The point $(4, 1)$ is rotated $90°$ clockwise about the origin. What is its image?
questions.solution: A rotation of $90°$ clockwise about the origin sends $(x, y)$ to $(y, -x)$, so $(4, 1)$ becomes $(1, -4)$. Anticlockwise would give $(-1, 4)$.

questions.prompt: The point $(4, 1)$ is enlarged by scale factor 2, centre the origin. Give the coordinates of the image.
questions.solution: With the centre at the origin, multiply both coordinates by the scale factor: $(8, 2)$.

questions.prompt: A shape is enlarged by scale factor $3$. How many times bigger is its area?
questions.solution: Every length is multiplied by $3$, and an area is made from two lengths, so it is multiplied by $3^2 = 9$. A volume would go up by $3^3 = 27$.

questions.prompt: A shape is made smaller by an enlargement. What can you say about the scale factor?
questions.solution: A scale factor between $0$ and $1$ shrinks the shape, and it is still called an enlargement. A negative factor would also flip it to the other side of the centre, which is a different thing from simply being smaller.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a complete description of a reflection?
questions.solution: A reflection is pinned down by the **equation** of its mirror line, so "reflection in the line $x = 2$" is complete. Naming no line, or giving a distance or a scale factor, does not identify the transformation.

questions.prompt: The point $(4, 1)$ is reflected in the line $y = x$. What is its image?
questions.solution: Reflecting in $y = x$ **swaps** the coordinates, so $(4, 1)$ becomes $(1, 4)$. The line $y = x$ is the diagonal through the origin, and each point sits the same distance from it on either side.

questions.prompt: Triangle $A$ has a vertex at $(4, 1)$. It is enlarged by scale factor 2 with centre $(1, 1)$. Give the coordinates of the image of that vertex.
questions.solution: Measure from the **centre**, not the origin. The vertex is $3$ across and $0$ up from $(1, 1)$. Doubling gives $6$ across and $0$ up, so the image is at $(1 + 6, 1) = (7, 1)$.

markScheme.description: measures 3 across from the centre and doubles it

questions.prompt: A triangle is enlarged by scale factor $-1$ about the origin. Which single transformation has exactly the same effect?
questions.solution: Scale factor $-1$ sends $(x, y)$ to $(-x, -y)$: same size, other side of the centre, upside down. That is exactly a rotation of $180°$ about the origin. Either single reflection would flip the order of the vertices, which a half turn does not.

questions.prompt: How do you find the centre of an enlargement, given the object and its image?
options: Take the midpoint of the two shapes
Use the origin, since it is always the centre
Measure the scale factor and count that many squares
Join matching vertices and extend the lines until they meet
questions.solution: Every line joining a vertex to its image passes through the centre, so drawing two or three of them and extending finds it exactly. This still works when the scale factor is fractional or negative, which is when guessing or using the midpoint breaks down.

questions.prompt: A shape is reflected in the $x$ axis and then in the $y$ axis. What single transformation has the same effect?
questions.solution: The first reflection sends $(x, y)$ to $(x, -y)$ and the second sends that to $(-x, -y)$. Both signs have changed, which is a rotation of $180°$ about the origin. Reflecting twice puts the vertices back in their original order, so the result is a rotation and not another reflection.

questions.prompt: An object and its image are the same size, but the vertices now run the opposite way round the shape. Which transformation was it?
questions.solution: A **reflection** is the only one of the four that reverses the order of the vertices. Translations and rotations slide or turn the shape while keeping that order, and an enlargement would have changed the size.

questions.prompt:
Triangle $A$ has vertices $(1, 1)$, $(4, 1)$ and $(1, 3)$, and an area of $3$ square units.

(a) Triangle $A$ is enlarged by scale factor $2$, centre the origin. Give the coordinates of the image, and its area.

(b) Triangle $A$ is enlarged by scale factor $2$, centre $(1, 1)$. Give the coordinates of this image.

(c) Explain what is the same and what is different about the two images.
questions.solution: For part a, the centre is the origin, so every coordinate is simply multiplied by the scale factor of two. One comma one becomes two comma two, four comma one becomes eight comma two, and one comma three becomes two comma six. For the area, lengths are multiplied by two, and an area is made from two lengths, so the area is multiplied by two squared, which is four. Three times four is twelve square units. For part b, the centre is now one comma one, so measure each vertex from there rather than from the origin. The vertex at one comma one is the centre itself, so it does not move at all. The vertex at four comma one is three across and nothing up from the centre; doubling gives six across, so the image is at seven comma one. The vertex at one comma three is nothing across and two up from the centre; doubling gives four up, so the image is at one comma five. For part c, what is the same is the size and shape: both images are triangles with a base of six and a height of four, so both have an area of twelve, and the two images are congruent to each other. What is different is where they sit. The scale factor decides how big the image is, but the centre decides where it goes, and moving the centre from the origin to one comma one has slid the whole image without changing it at all.

questions.prompt:
Triangle $A$ has vertices $(1, 1)$, $(4, 1)$ and $(1, 3)$.

(a) Rotate $A$ by $90°$ clockwise about the origin, and give the image coordinates.

(b) Rotate $A$ by $90°$ anticlockwise about the origin, and give the image coordinates.

(c) A student describes a transformation as "a rotation of $90°$ about the origin". Explain why this is not a complete description, using your answers to parts (a) and (b).
questions.solution: For part a, a rotation of ninety degrees clockwise about the origin sends the point x comma y to the point y comma minus x. Applying that to each vertex: one comma one becomes one comma minus one; four comma one becomes one comma minus four; and one comma three becomes three comma minus one. The image sits below the x axis. For part b, a rotation of ninety degrees anticlockwise about the origin sends x comma y to minus y comma x. So one comma one becomes minus one comma one; four comma one becomes minus one comma four; and one comma three becomes minus three comma one. This image sits to the left of the y axis. For part c, the student's description is incomplete because the two answers above are different triangles in different places, and yet both are rotations of ninety degrees about the origin. The clockwise image is below the x axis and the anticlockwise image is to the left of the y axis, so knowing only the angle and the centre does not tell you which of the two shapes is meant. A rotation therefore needs three things: the centre, the angle, and the direction. The one exception is a rotation of one hundred and eighty degrees, where turning clockwise and turning anticlockwise arrive at exactly the same place, so the direction can be left out.

examTechnique.body:
**Name the transformation first, then give its details.** Every mark scheme here is in two parts: the name, and the information that pins it down.

| Transformation | What must be given |
| --- | --- |
| Translation | the vector, as a column |
| Reflection | the equation of the mirror line |
| Rotation | centre, angle **and** direction |
| Enlargement | centre and scale factor |

**Give exactly one transformation.** "Reflection then translation" scores nothing when a single transformation was asked for. If the image is congruent and the same way round, try a rotation or a translation; if it has been flipped, try a reflection.

**Mirror lines are equations.** $x = 2$ is a vertical line; $y = 2$ is horizontal; $y = x$ is the diagonal. Saying "the mirror line" or "that line" earns nothing.

**For a rotation, always say clockwise or anticlockwise** — unless it is $180°$, where the two are the same and the direction can be omitted.

**To find a centre of rotation**, tracing paper is allowed and is the fastest method. To find a centre of enlargement, **join matching vertices and extend**.

**A negative scale factor** puts the image on the other side of the centre and turns it upside down. A **fractional** one makes it smaller, and it is still called an enlargement.

**Check with area.** If the scale factor is $3$, the image area must be $9$ times the object's.
examinerErrors: Describing a rotation without saying clockwise or anticlockwise.
Describing a reflection without giving the equation of the mirror line.
Giving two transformations when the question asked for one.
Writing a translation vector the wrong way round, so across and up are swapped.
Calling a shrinking an enlargement of scale factor $2$ rather than $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
Forgetting the centre of enlargement, so the image is the right size but in the wrong place.
Saying an enlargement of scale factor $3$ makes the area $3$ times bigger; it makes it $9$ times bigger.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer names the transformation and then gives every detail it needs, without being prompted: the vector, or the equation of the mirror line, or the centre with the angle and the direction, or the centre with the scale factor. It gives one transformation where one was asked for. It finds a centre of enlargement by joining matching vertices and extending rather than by guessing, which is the only method that survives a fractional or negative scale factor. It knows a negative scale factor flips the shape through the centre, and that an enlargement of scale factor k multiplies area by k squared. And it checks: if the image is a different size from the object, the answer cannot be a translation, a reflection or a rotation.
